articles.title: Limoges: Residents in shock after historic town hall set alight
articles.summary: A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests
articles.body:
A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday.

Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing.

On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse.

"Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC.

BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges.

articles.title: US Coast Guard rescues 16 people and searches for more after mayday call off Mexico's Baja coast
articles.summary: SAN DIEGO (AP) — Sixteen people were rescued from the Pacific Ocean off Mexico's Baja California coast on Friday after the U. Coast Guard responded to a mayd...
articles.body:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — Sixteen people were rescued from the Pacific Ocean off Mexico's Baja California coast on Friday after the U.S. Coast Guard responded to a mayday call reporting their boat was sinking. Another 11 people were believed missing.

The people rescued were Mexican nationals, according to the Mexican consulate. But the boat's origin, destination and what it was doing were not clear.

It went down in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants to the U.S. It's also popular with fishing and leisure boats.

One survivor was being treated for a suspected shark bite and two were in critical condition, authorities said.

A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours after someone on the boat transmitted a mayday call at about 1 a.m. to say it was sinking, said Coast Guard Lt. Santiago Tamburini. It took about 90 minutes for the crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, Tamburini said.

"People were holding onto each other, to debris, just treading and trying to stay above water before being rescued," he said.

The boat went down about 140 miles (225 kilometers) west of Ensenada, Mexico.

The search for more survivors across some 950 square nautical miles (3,200 square kilometers) was to continue overnight, officials said.

Survivors clung to debris, but the boat was gone

No vessel, only debris, was found and it was unclear what type of boat was involved, the Coast Guard said.

"Boats in that area can be for fishing, leisure, personal recreation. We just don't know what they were doing out there. We all know it's a suspected smuggling route," Tamburini said.

"The sea is unforgiving" in that area, he added, and it was unclear if the vessel got lost, had engine failure, was swept out to sea or meant to go that far.

Survivors said as many as 27 people had been on board, officials said. Some but not all of the people rescued were wearing life vests.

They rescued were flown by helicopter to San Diego and transported to hospitals. The Mexican consulate in San Diego said they were offered consular assistance.

Three were taken to Scripps Mercy Hospital San Diego, including the person with a suspected shark bite and two people treated for cold exposure, said hospital spokesperson Janice Collins. Three others were evaluated at Scripps Memorial Hospital La Jolla and later discharged, said Steve Carpowich, a Scripps Health spokesperson.

Two patients were in critical condition, said Matt Hoffman, a spokesperson for the city of San Diego. It was not clear if that included the suspected shark bite victim or the two people with cold exposure.

The search continues for 11 missing people

The Coast Guard and U.S. Navy were searching the area with two helicopters, a fixed-wing plane, a cutter and a Navy combat ship.

The Mexican Navy also launched a search and rescue operation from Ensenada, which is about 80 miles (130 kilometers) south of San Diego by road.

"As long as we think it's viable, we will continue to search," said Coast Guard Capt. Rob Tucker.

Conditions on the water at 1 a.m. Friday appeared to be windy but fairly typical for the area, according to National Weather Service meteorologist Jonathan Suk in San Diego. Winds out of the north and northwest measured about 10 knots (18.5 kilometers per hour) and waves measured 5 feet (1.5 meters) at a buoy north of Ensenada, he said.

"I wouldn't want to be out there in a sea kayak," Suk said. "For the vessels that usually operate out there, they're usually built to handle things like that."

The water temperature measured 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 degrees Celsius) -- fairly warm for the Pacific -- and the air was 70 degrees Fahrenheit (21 degrees Celsius), Suk said.

Deadly smuggling accidents have struck these waters before

Migrants are increasingly turning to the risky alternative offered by smugglers to travel by sea to avoid heavily guarded land borders. Small boats called pangas leave Baja at night and sometimes travel hundreds of miles (kilometers) north.

There have been several episodes where migrant vessels capsized en route to California in recent years.

In May of 2025, at least three people died when a panga flipped off the coast about 35 miles (56 km) north of the U.S.-Mexico border. In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the U.S. coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog and one capsized in the surf.

A federal judge sentenced a San Diego man to 18 years in prison in 2022 for piloting a small vessel overloaded with 32 migrants that smashed apart in powerful surf off the coast, killing three people and injuring more than two dozen.

Watson reported from Los Angeles and Brown from Billings, Montana. Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, Fabiola Sanchez in Mexico City and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, contributed to this story.

articles.title: The women playing Australia's biggest sport - in London
articles.summary: From London beginners to Australian pros, women are helping Aussie Rules thrive in the capital.
articles.body:
London-born Iona Williams has only visited Australia a handful of times, but that hasn't stopped her becoming a regular player of one of the nation's most-viewed sports.

The 29-year-old discovered Australian Rules Football in her home city after a friend suggested she try it out. She had never played before, and didn't know the rules, but five years on she's a key feature of her club, the West London Wildcats.

"The team were really welcoming," she told the BBC, "Everyone's really together and always so keen to help each other and kind of make each other better at the sport."

Iona is emblematic of a growing appreciation for the sport both amongst women and outside of Australia.

Although women only started playing the sport professionally in Australia for the first time in 2017, the sport has spread internationally - the League estimates that about 75,000 women and girls participate outside of the country.

London boasts its own Australian Football League, with teams playing across two divisions.

"I would say it's like Gaelic football, regular football - like soccer - and rugby all kind of combined", explains Iona.

Known as Australian Rules Football (AFL), Aussie Rules or Footy, it originated in Australia and has been played there for more than 150 years.

The game takes place on an oval-shaped field, where two teams try to get more points than the other by kicking goals or behinds. Unlike in other sports, players can use both their hands and feet as they move by punching the ball, running with the ball, or kicking it.

Footy has a reputation for being ferocious - in 2022 an American went viral for his description of the game: "These guys are angry all the time, probably because they're running a marathon during a fistfight".

But Iona says any Londoners intimidated by the sport should try out regardless: "Don't be scared to get involved.

"There's so many girls that start that have never played before - me included."

Being the most watched sport in Australia, AFL London's clubs provide a familiar comfort for the well-established community of Australians in the city.

"I played back in Australia for a fair few years so it's just such an easy jump. You know you're going to meet Aussies and walk into a new brand new bunch of friends," says Jamie Symons, 27, who moved from Tasmania to London two years ago.

However, the league is careful to prevent Australians dominating the clubs. In the Women's Prem (top division), there needs to be four non-Aussie players on the field (which could comprise of two on the interchange bench).

"It is awesome to see these British people embracing the game, especially playing in their country. It's really exciting," Jamie says.

"It's nice to make British friends as well, not just have all these Aussies in an AFL club."

Jamie plays alongside Iona at the West London Wildcats, and the pair have embraced both the sporting and social opportunities it offers.

From pub crawls, barbecues, and a ladies' day (where they celebrate the women of the club), playing footy has meant getting to mingle with people from different backgrounds.

"Whenever I ask for a sausage sandwich, it's now called a snag", says Iona, referencing the Australian colloquialisms she's learnt.

Playing Aussie rules in London can also be a pipeline to a professional career in Australia.

Kate Shierlaw, like Jamie, sought out AFL while she was living in London.

She played for the Wimbledon Hawks before being recruited to play professionally in Australia.

Kate, who now plays for North Melbourne, was happy to hear that women across the world continue to enjoy the sport she loves.

"It's super special. I think because I started there, being able to see so many people playing over there, playing the best sport in the world, it's really exciting," she said.

Women only officially joined the AFL London league 26 years after its male counterpart which was established in 1989 and enjoyed its inaugural season in 1990.

Despite the decades-long delay, the AFL claim women's football in London has seen "significant growth" within the last decade.

"The inaugural AFL London women's competition commenced in 2015, featuring four founding teams. In 2026, the competition comprised ten teams across two divisions," wrote Kaitlyn Blanchard, media manager at AFLW in a statement to the BBC.

"Female participation in Australian Football programs and competitions outside Australia grew by approximately 35% between 2023 and 2025," she wrote noting strong female participation in Papua New Guinea, South Africa, and Fiji.

Kate Shierlaw hopes to see this growth continue.

"We should be sharing the sport all over the world so it's so good to see so many girls playing."

articles.title: Aberfan disaster: The portraits that helped bring the children home
articles.summary: An artist living hundreds of miles away felt compelled to help the village that lost its children.
articles.body:
For almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village.

Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique.

The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings.

In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits , some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve.

"It brought her back to life," said Denise Morgan, whose younger sister Annette was among those who died in the Aberfan disaster.

On 21 October 1966, a coal tip collapsed above the village. The torrent of slurry engulfed Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes, killing 144 people including 116 children.

The disaster remains woven into everyday life in Aberfan. It is felt most strongly in the memorial garden on the site of the fallen school, and among the white arched monuments of the cemetery.

But it's also felt in the empty places left behind at family tables, in childhood bedrooms which were suddenly occupied by one child instead of two, and in the portraits that came to represent those who never grew up.

Jeanette Keane has fond memories of her sister Edwina.

"It was just such an idyllic childhood really," she said. "She was very quiet and gentle. She had a mischievous streak as well."

The morning of the disaster remains painfully vivid, as Jeanette recalled how Edwina quickly returned home before the school day had begun.

"She came running back and she said, 'Mammy, I forgot to give you a kiss'," Jeanette said. "And so my mother gave her a kiss.

"My mother always said that, at that time, she wanted to keep her home.

"And my mother rued that day for the rest of her life. She just wished she'd listened to herself."

Jeanette's father found eight-year-old Edwina trapped beneath the wreckage.

"She was alive," Jeanette said, but it was a heartbreaking situation.

"He couldn't get her out because the roof would have fallen in.

"The men all said, 'Teddy, you can't,' and my father laid by the side of her, held her hand and she suffocated."

The trauma echoed through the years that followed the disaster.

"It explains to me why we used to hear him walking back and fore in the corridor at night, banging his head on the wall," Jeanette said.

"It wasn't a very happy life afterwards. Everything changed."

Denise Morgan was attending a different school when word began to spread that something terrible had happened in Aberfan, where her little sister Annette was in class.

"They didn't really give us any details," she said. Racing off the train, the devastation was clear. "When we looked across to Aberfan, we could just see this black mass."

As rescue efforts began, families across the village waited for news. Some of the memories remain too painful to revisit.

For the surviving siblings, that sense of loss seemed to arrive in the most ordinary moments.

"We always slept together," said Jeanette. "And suddenly I was alone."

"We shared a bed... and then she was gone."

The scale of grief was impossible to escape. "In our street, five children were lost in 25 houses," Denise said.

"Four children died in my street," Jeanette recalled.

In an era when grief was rarely discussed openly, many survivors were left to process the tragedy alone.

Hundreds of miles away in Llandudno, one man was following events in Aberfan on television and in the newspapers.

Artist William Richardson had no connection to Aberfan, with his skills being used most often on the pier where he sketched caricatures of visitors and celebrities performing in town.

But he was deeply affected by what he saw. According to his children, Jean and Ken, he felt compelled to do something for the bereaved families who had lost their sons and daughters.

"He saw it on the news and he was so moved by it, he decided to paint them," Jean said.

"He just wanted to give something back, to show he cared," added Ken.

Richardson never sought payment or recognition. Instead, he began creating portraits of children killed in the disaster, working from school photographs and detailed descriptions supplied by parents.

"The parents would write to him and tell him about the children," Jean said. "What colour their eyes were, their hair, what they wore."

"They even sent bits of fabric so he could get it right," Ken added.

Jean said her father wanted to capture more than their appearance.

"He'd ask about their personalities, so he could build that into the painting."

Over the years, Richardson is believed to have produced about 100 portraits. As the collection grew, so too did his connection with families in Aberfan.

For his children, the portraits became a constant presence.

"We were surrounded by them for years," said Jean. "All these faces."

"It's like looking back at old friends now."

"We couldn't believe the likeness," Denise said. "That was her.

Jeanette remembered the effect on her parents when Edwina's portrait arrived.

"I remember my father crying when the painting came," she said. "If they could have hugged it, they would have."

The portraits soon became part of daily life in homes across the village.

"She was there at Christmas, at parties, always in the room," Denise said of Annette's painting.

For survivors such as Gaynor Madgwick, who escaped from Pantglas Junior School when the tip collapsed, the images served another purpose.

"They start conversations," she said. "People begin talking about their children again."

For families who had struggled to find the words, the portraits offered a way to keep memories alive.

"You walked in and their presence was there," Gaynor said.

Jeanette agreed: "It was very, very important to us. It felt like she was always with us while it was there."

As the generation directly affected by Aberfan grows older, a new question is emerging: what should happen to the portraits?

Many remain cherished family possessions. Others have already passed into the care of younger generations, while some have been entrusted to a local museum.

Other families have made different choices.

Gaynor described the heartbreaking decision her family faced after their mother died.

"Taking them down, you're not taking a painting, you're taking them," she said.

The portraits were buried alongside their mother.

"We buried them with Mam in a white box, like a little coffin.

For Jeanette, the future of Edwina's portrait is a source of concern.

"I worry about what will happen to the painting," she said. "I want people to see them."

Denise feels the same pull between preservation and possession.

"It's a treasure," she said. "I could never part with it."

Nearly six decades after the disaster, the paintings remain extraordinary objects. They were created by a man who had never met the children, but his kindness ensured they were treasured by the families who received and loved them.

By painstakingly recreating the faces of children who had been lost, William Richardson gave something precious back to a community living with unimaginable grief.

For many families, the portraits did more than capture memories. They brought the children home.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The bail hearing of Cockroach Janta Party functionaries Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka was put off Sunday after the special executive magistrate failed to arrive at the scheduled time, and later recused himself citing threat to his life.Delhi police registered a case in connection with the alleged threat. Police sources said the SEM had been pressured to release Ranka and Das without delay.CJP argued that the alleged threat was a separate complaint and suggested that police examine call detail records (CDRs) to ascertain whether the SEM’s number had been shared from a CJP member’s device. She posted on X that said she had been at the police station since 11am for the hearing, which was scheduled for noon, but the assistant commissioner of police, who also functions as the SEM, arrived around 5.30pm.Advocate Abhist Hela said no specific statutory provision was cited to reschedule the hearing, with the decision resting on concerns for judicial officers’ safety, among others.“Someone tried to influence him, and he (SEM) recused himself from the hearing today. articles.title: Northern Ireland Troubles Bill to be debated in House of Commons
articles.summary: The government has published hundreds of amendments, including that the attorney general must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the conflict.
articles.body:
Labour's Northern Ireland Troubles Bill will return to the House of Commons later on Monday for hours of debate before MPs vote on proposed changes to the legislation.

Last week, the government published hundreds of amendments, including that the attorney general must provide consent for any serious prosecutions related to the Troubles under the new plan.

The legislation seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict which cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.

It has been more than a year since it was first introduced to Parliament, following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government.

A debate known as the "committee of the whole house" will take place on Monday, with its remaining Commons' stages on Tuesday.

If it is passed by MPs, it will then move to the House of Lords for further consideration.

NI Secretary defends planned changes to Troubles bill

Attorney general approval required for serious Troubles prosecutions

New legislation on Troubles legacy deal introduced in Westminster

The government has defended the changes it is hoping to get support for, with Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant saying the bill will help provide answers for many families.

However, it has received a mixed response from political parties in Northern Ireland, as well as from victims and veterans' groups.

Sinn Féin said the plans amounted to a "veterans' charter", while the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) accused the government of seeking to rush through the bill without a proper chance for MPs to scrutinise it.

Mark Thompson from the victims' group Relatives For Justice said he feared the bill could lead to unlawful killings being covered up by the state.

"Essentially, this impacts the victims of collusion and state violence," he told the BBC's Sunday Politics programme .

He accused the government of trying to take "control" away from local courts because it did not like some of the recent rulings in Troubles-era cases.

He pointed out that judges had ruled against the Army in "dozens" of inquests into killings carried out by soldiers, including those at Ballymurphy and Springhill .

Thompson argued that local courts had provided a "level playing field" but instead the government caved under pressure from the Army veterans' lobby in London.

"What they [the government] want to do is lift it out of a rule of law process and bring it to London and have a political decision."

However, lawyer Philip Barden, who has represented several ex-soldiers, claimed Army veterans were "put through the mill" in cases where there was "no evidence".

"What we want is an independent process so its not the PPS and the DPP deciding in Northern Ireland who it is who should be prosecuted," Barden told the programme.

"We, frankly, wanted a Supreme Court judge as being the most independent person that we could conceive of - not being a political appointment.

"The government have come up with the attorney general of the UK, who of course makes many decisions to prosecute people."

Barden defended the government's choice, saying if people disagreed with the UK attorney general's decisions they could always seek a judicial review.

"So there is complete independence," he argued.

He added that veterans' "primary cause of concern" was the number of repeat investigations into Troubles cases, despite a lack of any new or compelling evidence.

It seeks to replace the previous Conservative government's contentious 2023 Legacy Act , which introduced a ban on inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era incidents.

The act's most controversial element - offering immunity from prosecution to suspects who cooperated with an information recovery body - was disapplied after being found by the courts to be unlawful.

Labour's bill involves a legacy commission to investigate Troubles-related killings, a separate information recovery body, and a dedicated legacy unit within An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

The government said its amendments "significantly reduce" the prospect of military veterans facing "rinse and repeat" investigations.

While some MPs have previously argued that planned protections for veterans do not go far enough, Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has accused the government of giving former soldiers "preferential treatment".

What is the government proposing to change?

The legislation will make clear the commission and coroners "must not regard the lawful conduct of members of the armed forces as equivalent to the actions of paramilitaries responsible for acts of terrorism"

The attorney general, currently Ellie Reeves, will be required to consent to all "serious" Troubles-related prosecutions

There would be measures to prevent "cold-calling" of veterans and extending provisions for remote attendance as part of the commission's work

Before any witness can be approached, the commission should consider if "compelling new evidence exists, or the likelihood of a witness being able to provide new information"

The commission must consider the "context and command orders" in which military veterans were operating

Former paramilitaries are barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors Advisory Group, and there is a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans' representative to be on the panel

There is a statutory review of the measures for veterans to ensure they "deliver as intended"

Opposition parties and backbench MPs have also tabled separate amendments aimed at changing the bill, but it is up to the Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle to decide whether any of them will be accepted for debate.

articles.title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove
articles.summary: More property asking prices are being cut than at any time in 15 years, data shared with the BBC shows.
articles.body:
Home sellers cut asking prices on more than 3,000 properties a day on average in Britain during September, according to figures from Rightmove shared exclusively with the BBC.

The property website said the total was the highest of any month for 15 years and was driven, in part, by a glut of homes on the market and some sellers setting unrealistic expectations.

The proportion of listed homes that eventually had a price cut peaked in 2023 and has remained relatively high since.

Property portals say buyers are now having to be choosy, with many working to a tight budget as mortgage rates have risen to three-year highs.

"Once a home has been on the market for a while and then has a price reduction, some buyers start asking questions, even when there is nothing wrong with the property," said Colleen Babcock of Rightmove.

"In a market with so much choice, first impressions matter."

Rightmove data said the average price reduction was nearly 7% - the equivalent of nearly £21,000 cut from a typically valued home.

Its data showed that homes that had a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for those listed at one price.

The proportion of listed homes that had a price reduction stood at 34% in last month, only slightly lower than the recent peak of 36% seen in September 2023.

Rival property portal Zoopla said that buyers were in the driving seat, and were being more cautious and selective about the properties they viewed.

With mortgage rates at a three-year high , Zoopla said buyers needed to keep monthly mortgage payments affordable.

So, while the number of homes for sale was up 5% in September compared with a year earlier, the number of sales agreed had fallen by 9% over the same period, its figures showed.

September also tends to be the month with the most cuts to asking prices as sellers often want to complete a sale by the end of the year.

Zoopla's data showed that a quarter of newly-listed homes in September had previously been listed for sale in the last year. Six in 10 were returning at a lower asking price.

The problem for sellers was that these homes were taking longer to sell.

Properties that needed a price reduction were half as likely to find a buyer within the normal three-month timeframe, according to Richard Donnell, executive director of research at Rightmove.

'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?

You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it

Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England.

One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier."

Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".

But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.

Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial.

"That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.

Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price.

"The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.

But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.

In Scotland, the Home Report system requires an independent valuation of a home before it is put on the market.

Donnell, from Zoopla, said the system gave sellers a guide to pricing. As a result homes sold at a faster rate than anywhere else in Britain.

His data showed that 74% of homes in Scotland listed during April, May and June sold within three months, compared with 30% in London.

He said that higher prices, stamp duty and some people - including landlords - not needing to sell meant that listed homes were less likely to sell in southern England.

Graphics by BBC data journalist Tommy Lumby

articles.title: CBS reporter deletes post calling out El-Sayed on 'spectacular self own' on Muslim Brotherhood question
articles.summary: CBS News correspondent Jan Crawford deleted her post criticizing Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's townhall response about the Muslim Brotherhood.
articles.body: CBS News correspondent Jan Crawford deleted an X post that appeared to attack Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his viral response to a question on the Muslim Brotherhood. During a town hall on Saturday, El-Sayed responded to a voter named Tommy who asked him whether he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood after reports about El-Sayed's alleged family connections to the organization. "Why would you actually think that about me? Why would you actually think that? Why would you? Have you asked everybody in your life if they disavow them [the Muslim Brotherhood]? So why are you asking me?" El-Sayed said. El-Sayed later shared a clip of the interaction with his followers. "This is Tommy. Tommy had a question about my allegiances. Listen to the end to hear about his," El-Sayed wrote. CBS CHIEF BARI WEISS' INVOLVEMENT IN VIRAL EL-SAYED REPORT SPARKS DEBATE AMONG CRITICS Crawford was initially critical of El-Sayed's response, suggesting that Tommy succeeded in "triggering" the candidate. His subsequent uninterrupted three-minute diatribe proving your exact point is the kind of spectacular self own most ppl only dream about triggering. Congrats," Crawford wrote. I deleted that tweet because it was a violation of CBS News standards. I apologize," Crawford wrote. CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS The initial post sparked backlash from pundits and analysts on the left, several of whom called for Crawford to be fired. "No Jan — you got caught red handed trying to help prop up a paid GOP operative who was there to spread false, racist lies about Abdul because he is Muslim. Shame on you," Democratic consultant Karen Finney replied to Crawford. "She SHOULD be fired, but it's CBS news, so she'll get promoted," progressive commentator and Democratic strategist Ketih Edwards wrote. "This woman endorsing a GOP operative’s smear campaign against @AbdulElSayed is apparently a ‘straight news’ CBS reporter. This is what David Ellison paid for. This is what Bari Weiss delivered," Zeteo CEO Mehdi Hasan posted. A CBS News spokesperson cited Crawford’s statement and declined to comment further. Curtis Houck, managing editor of media watchdog NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital that those calling for Crawford to be fired over the post "need to grow up." "The double standard is glaring. Reporters from CNN, MS NOW, The New York Times, and Washington Post tweet all kinds of incendiary hot takes on the daily, and none of the elitist media defenders bat an eye. But for someone at Bari Weiss's CBS News to call out the tone of a Democrat? It's unforgivable. Jan should be allowed to speak her mind and has earned it as one of the few actual journalists on the networks, in addition to a long career covering the Supreme Court, and earned the trust of the justices. Team Bari Weiss needs to tell these people calling for Jan's job to shove it," he continued. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment. In a previous statement to Fox News, his campaign called these allegations "racist and untrue." However, El-Sayed confirmed to Fox News senior correspondent Mike Tobin on Saturday that his sister-in-law, Mariam Jukaku, was involved in a federal terrorist watchlist lawsuit in 2016. "She did nothing wrong and was captured on that and then sued and got off," El-Sayed said. "You've got this system where folks are guilty until proven innocent because they've got different kinds of names, because of the infrastructure that people like Mike Rogers set up."

articles.title: Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams
articles.summary: Trading standards officers say AI is "super-charging" existing scams through clones and fake websites.
articles.body:
Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.

Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.

If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say.

AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.

For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low cost

Romance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or months

AI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency"

Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scale

Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.

Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?.

Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include:

Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person

Doing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using the Financial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker , to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is real

Not assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video call

In general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think.

Fraud and scams can be reported to Report Fraud or by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice.

articles.title: Phone on speaker in train? You may be penalised, jailed
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a move that could bring relief to railway passengers disturbed by people playing music or watching videos on their phones in speaker mode
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a move that could bring relief to railway passengers disturbed by people playing music or watching videos on their phones in speaker mode and check the growing menace, Southern Railway has warned that such behaviour could attract a penalty of Rs 1,000 and lead to removal from railway premises, including coaches. People persisting with such an act could even face up to six months of jail and up to Rs 5,000 penalty.Southern Railway has invoked Section 142 of the Railways Act, as amended under the Jan Vishwas Act, to enforce provisions dealing with causing a nuisance.Officials said that the provision can be invoked by other railway zones and even by Metro systems to check such behaviour, which adversely affects the comfort of other passengers. As per law, creating a nuisance in Metro rail also attracts a penalty and such persons can be removed from coaches.Section 270 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) defines public nuisance as an act that causes common injury, danger, obstruction or annoyance to people using a public right and hence amounts to an offence.In a circular issued to all its divisions this month and marked to Railway Board, Southern Railway flagged the problem of passengers playing music or audio through speakers at railway stations and inside trains, describing it as a “nuisance”.The circular also referred to a Railway Board communication issued in July 2012 on the use of mobile phones. The board had flagged issues such as “loud talking, lengthy conversations” and sound of objectionable ringtones inside coaches and asked all zones to create awareness against such practices.Official communication from Southern Zone stated, “In recent times, with the advent of widespread mobile internet access, the playing of videos and other content in speaker mode is highly prevalent in public spaces. ln the present scenario, there is urgent need to put in place arrangements in order to ensure that travelling passengers are not inconvenienced.”It has directed its divisions to educate passengers on the relevant legal provisions and discourage them from playing music or videos in speaker mode or engaging in loud conversations while travelling or on railway premises. Awareness campaigns are to be conducted through public address systems in regional languages, Hindi and English. It has said that ticket examiners and other senior officials from commercial division can impose the Rs 1,000 penalty on offenders.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Conheça tecnologia do Coliseu de Roma usada para monitorar estrutura do Museu do Ipiranga, na Zona Sul de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: A tecnologia de escaneamento a laser em 3D, já utilizada na Itália, foi aplicada no Museu do Ipiranga para criar uma representação digital do edifício histórico e ajudar a prevenir problemas estruturais sem interromper a visitação pública.
articles.summary: A tecnologia de escaneamento a laser em 3D, já utilizada na Itália, foi aplicada no Museu do Ipiranga para criar uma representação digital do edifício histórico e ajudar a prevenir problemas estruturais sem interromper a visitação pública.
articles.body:
Aparelho emite raios laser, capta a variação de luz e revela desníveis e até mofos — Foto: Lucas Cerejo/TV Globo

Pesquisadores brasileiros adotaram uma tecnologia de escaneamento 3D a laser usada no Coliseu, em Roma, para monitorar a integridade estrutural do Museu do Ipiranga, em São Paulo .

O trabalho mapeou cada milímetro do prédio histórico, por dentro e por fora, e permite acompanhar o comportamento da edificação após a reforma que manteve o espaço fechado por nove anos. A tecnologia também possibilita criar um modelo digital do museu para auxiliar na preservação preventiva do patrimônio.

O projeto é uma parceria entre a Universidade de São Paulo (USP) e a Universidade de Ferrara, na Itália. A execução ficou a cargo de pesquisadores italianos da mesma equipe que escaneou o Coliseu. As duas instituições mantêm uma parceria de pesquisa há 20 anos.

O trabalho durou três semanas, entre setembro e outubro deste ano, e foi realizado de forma gradual para não interferir na rotina do museu. Os espaços maiores, como o Salão Nobre, foram escaneados às segundas-feiras, quando não recebem visitantes.

Projeto de escaneamento 3D a laser cria uma representação digital do prédio histórico — Foto: Lucas Cerejo/TV Globo

Os pesquisadores utilizam um equipamento portátil, do tamanho de uma caixa de sapato, que emite raios laser para registrar as coordenadas de cada ponto das paredes, dos pisos e das fachadas. As informações são reunidas em um grande arquivo digital.

Diferentemente da medição tradicional, feita com trenas e baseada nos ângulos principais de uma sala, o laser registra a superfície real com precisão de milímetros. O equipamento capta variações e revela desníveis, grau de umidade e até pequenos sinais de mofo nas paredes.

Para o professor de Arquitetura da Universidade de Ferrara, Marcello Balzani, o processo funciona como um exame médico detalhado.

“O edifício respira e se transforma com o tempo. É como fazer uma radiografia, um ultrassom, uma tomografia. A estrutura são os ossos, os caminhos são os músculos, o ar são os pulmões. Temos essa relação corpórea com a arquitetura. E, em uma edificação histórica, isso é ainda mais importante: precisamos mantê-la com saúde”, explica Balzani.

Modelo digital permite comparar antes e depois

A equipe italiana já havia escaneado o museu entre 2017 e 2018, antes da obra de restauração do edifício. O novo levantamento permite comparar as condições da estrutura antes e depois da reforma.

O resultado é um modelo tridimensional conhecido como “gêmeo digital”, que reúne informações físicas do prédio. O processo é chamado de HBIM, sigla em inglês para Modelagem de Informação da Construção Histórica.

“No modelo digital do museu, nós vamos anotando todas as manutenções e tentando descobrir as causas. Se uma lâmpada queima a cada três meses é porque tem alguma coisa errada com a instalação. Assim, é possível intervir antes de a situação se agravar”, explica Beatriz Kühl, professora da Faculdade de Arquitetura e Urbanismo e Design (FAU-USP) e coordenadora científica do projeto Ipiranga Digital.

O mapa virtual também permite simular cenários extremos provocados pelas mudanças climáticas, como temporais mais fortes e dias de calor intenso, para avaliar como o prédio pode reagir. Antecipar problemas custa menos, evita obras pesadas e reduz a necessidade de intervenções no patrimônio histórico.

Tecnologia já foi usada no Coliseu de Roma

Museu do Ipiranga guarda um acervo com mais de 450 mil itens — Foto: Lucas Cerejo/TV Globo

A tecnologia aplicada no Museu do Ipiranga já foi utilizada no Coliseu, em Roma, que recebe cerca de 30 mil visitantes por dia. Na Itália, a equipe precisou documentar milênios de intervenções sobrepostas à estrutura original do monumento .

O trabalho gerou cerca de 150 terabytes de informações , processadas por máquinas e analisadas pelos pesquisadores.

“Mais do que a tecnologia, vale o conhecimento das pessoas. O scanner não faz nada sozinho. O diferencial está sempre na capacitação técnica de quem interpreta os dados e extrai sentido daquelas informações. É necessário o talento humano organizando o processo para que a inteligência artificial possa cruzar essas informações a nosso favor. Afinal, quem dá o laudo médico é o médico, e não a máquina”, reforça Balzani.

Museu do Ipiranga guarda mais de 450 mil itens

Jardim do Museu do Ipiranga, na Zona Sul de SP — Foto: Paola Patriarca/g1

Projetado como um monumento para celebrar a Independência do Brasil, o Museu do Ipiranga foi construído entre 1885 e 1890 e inaugurado em 7 de setembro de 1895. Com 130 anos de história, é o museu público mais antigo da capital paulista e é tombado como patrimônio histórico municipal, estadual e federal.

O acervo reúne mais de 450 mil itens, entre objetos, fotografias e documentos do século 17 até meados do século 20, importantes para a compreensão da sociedade brasileira.

Entre os móveis e as obras de arte, destaca-se a tela “Independência ou Morte”, do pintor Pedro Américo. Feita em 1888, a pintura representa livremente o momento em que Dom Pedro I teria proclamado a separação do Brasil de Portugal.

Professores Beatriz Kühl, da FAU-USP, e Marcello Balzani, Universidade de Ferrara, coordenam o projeto — Foto: Lucas Cerejo/TV Globo

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
articles.body:
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.

One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.

There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."

And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.

It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine

Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.

"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.

His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.

"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.

He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.

If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.

"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".

But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.

Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.

Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.

"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."

But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

articles.title: Milan on edge: Protesters clash with cops, smash windows; videos show chaos
articles.summary: Milan descended into chaos on Sunday as hundreds of masked protesters clashed with police, smashed shop windows and looted stores in the city centre, with
articles.body: Milan descended into chaos on Sunday as hundreds of masked protesters clashed with police, smashed shop windows and looted stores in the city centre, with videos showing tense scenes around the iconic Piazza del Duomo. The violence erupted during demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services, a day after similar unrest swept several Italian cities.According to Italian news outlet Il Post, groups of youths, many of them minors, moved through central Milan, throwing firecrackers, damaging property and breaking into shops along Via Torino, around Piazza Duomo and in the Castello district. Several tram shelters were smashed, while scooters, tables and rubbish bins were overturned. Protesters also targeted a window at the Rinascente department store and threw stones at the windows of a McDonald's outlet.Videos circulating on social media showed crowds scattering through Piazza del Duomo amid clouds of smoke, with police vehicles surrounded by demonstrators and officers confronting groups in the square.Reuters reported that police in riot gear used tear gas and water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters smashed shop windows and set rubbish bins on fire near Piazza Duomo. According to sources cited by the news agency, more than 60 protesters were taken to police stations for further checks.Il Post reported that more than 200 youths had been stopped and taken to police stations by Sunday evening, with around 80% of them believed to be minors, according to police sources. Several had already been identified during Saturday's unrest. Police also moved towards Via Meravigli and Piazzale Cadorna, where further disturbances were reported. Around 10 people were stopped near San Babila after attempting to flee from officers in riot gear.The latest violence followed clashes on Saturday in Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin. According to a police report cited by Reuters, 28 protesters were arrested following Saturday's confrontations.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence and announced a meeting on public order at Palazzo Chigi on Monday to discuss further measures against those exploiting demonstrations to cause unrest.Milan mayor Giuseppe Sala also acknowledged the grievances behind the protests while condemning the destruction, saying the reasons for demonstrating were understandable but violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city were unjustifiable.The unrest in Italy unfolded alongside violent demonstrations in neighbouring France and Belgium, where anger over rising living costs and public services also triggered clashes, looting and confrontations with security forces.You use AI every day. articles.body: It is said that often truth is the first casualty of war. This is increasingly becoming true of political contests as well, where post-truth politics is emerging as an important dimension of public discourse.In the post-truth scenario, false propaganda, distorted narratives, and emotional appeals devoid of logic often take precedence over objective facts and verifiable evidence. And, reasoned debate gives way to demagoguery.Once largely a subject of academic debates, post-truth has now become a feature of everyday politics. Misinformation campaigns designed to gaslight are increasingly used to not only sway public opinion but also discredit democratic institutions.Allegations are repeated and amplified even when the evidence to substantiate them is conspicuously absent. In this, truth seems to be not merely the first casualty, but it risks becoming the final casualty as well.India’s political discourse is not immune to this post-truth phenomenon. Increasingly, sections of the opposition parties appear to be manufacturing outrage, peddling propaganda and weaponising misinformation to spread anarchy, placing avaricious political goals above national interests.The article does not aim a jeremiad against the opposition nor a claim that constitutional institutions are beyond criticism. Dissent is the lifeblood of democracy. What it is not is a licence to peddle falsehoods. Disagreement is necessary for better policymaking. What it is not is a pass for vindictive and sustained assault on public trust through allegations that crumble under factual scrutiny.The purpose, therefore, is to challenge these falsehoods and restore public trust in constitutional institutions, which has been eroded by the cynical politics of manufactured distrust.This becomes particularly significant when we examine how electoral institutions and processes have been attacked by certain sections of opposition to hide the fact that people are rejecting them again and again.Three issues, in particular, stand out: the recurring allegations of manipulation of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), the controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and unscrupulous attempts to discredit the Election Commission of India (ECI).First things first, EVMs have repeatedly been subjected to allegations of manipulation by the opposition. The Supreme Court has examined such challenges on multiple occasions. Finally, in 2024, in its ‘Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India’, the Supreme Court put to rest all doubts and rejected demands for a return to paper ballots. The Supreme Court observed that repeated challenges based on suspicion and doubt, without cogent material or data, were “execrable and undesirable”. But this could not stop the opposition from repeating the same lies again and again.The controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls is another example of how a legally right and administratively justified exercise has been impugned for narrow political interests by some in this post-truth era.In 2025, the Supreme Court in its ‘Association for Democratic Reforms v. Election Commission of India’ judgment, affirmed that the integrity of electoral rolls is foundational to free and fair elections. It described the objective of ensuring the “accuracy, completeness, and integrity of the electoral roll” as “not only legitimate but is integral to the constitutional mandate” entrusted to the Commission.The Court also found that the reasons advanced for the revision bore a “direct and rational nexus” to maintaining a credible electoral process. These observations reinforced a fundamental principle: protecting the right to vote requires not only safeguarding every eligible voter, but also ensuring that electoral rolls remain accurate, complete and reliable.Beyond EVMs and SIR, a sustained campaign has been run to discredit the office of the Chief Election Commissioner, and by extension the institution of the Election Commission of India (ECI).For nearly seven decades, Congress governments retained executive control over the appointment of Chief Election Commissioner. Our government changed this by institutionalising the appointment process through a multi-member Selection Committee that includes the Leader of the Opposition.The record of Congress has been far from inspiring when it comes to respecting the independence of other constitutional institutions as well.In 1951, the then government introduced the First Constitutional Amendment to reverse Supreme Court judgment and curtailed freedom of speech and expression.During the Emergency, constitutional amendments were weaponised to serve the interests of the government. The amendments made the proclamation of Emergency non-justiciable and placed the Prime Minister’s election beyond judicial scrutiny. It also granted sweeping immunity to high constitutional functionaries and curtailed judicial review. The amendment power was turned from an instrument of constitutional reform into a tool for executive aggrandisement.Not only institutions were trampled but human rights of citizens were also violated. Attorney General Niren De, representing the then Union Government, argued in the Supreme Court that even if an innocent person was killed by a police officer acting out of personal enmity, the victim’s family could not seek judicial relief.Now, compare this with how the Constitution has been honoured in the last 12 years under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, passed by a special majority of Parliament, was struck down by the Supreme Court. The verdict was not only respected, but no attempt was made to overturn it through backdoor legislation. This respect for the Constitution and its principles has also guided our approach to some of the most consequential issues facing the nation.The construction of the Ram Mandir began only after the Supreme Court’s judgment. When Article 370 was abrogated and the Supreme Court upheld the decision, many in the opposition still disagreed with the judgment.Even legislative processes and offices have not been spared by the Congress. A no-confidence motion was moved against the Lok Sabha Speaker when he simply asked the Leader of opposition to follow the rules.Post-truth politics has also extended to matters of national security. In 2019, the Congress leader wrongly attributed a slogan to the Supreme Court’s Rafale judgment and later tendered an unconditional apology in contempt proceedings. In August 2025, the Supreme Court again questioned the basis of claims made by Rahul Gandhi regarding the occupation of Indian territory, asking what credible evidence supported them.Respecting differences of opinion has always been an integral part of our democratic ethos. When people raised concerns over the three farm laws passed by Parliament, we not only listened to those concerns but also repealed the laws in the larger public interest.In a democracy, one is free to disagree with a decision. But such disagreements cannot be founded on falsehoods, nor can their purpose be to create disorder and anarchy. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, in his famous speech in the Constituent Assembly, often referred to as the “Grammar of Anarchy,” warned against the dangers of resorting to unconstitutional methods.His message remains profoundly relevant today. Opposition leaders would do well to read this historic speech and understand the crucial distinction between dissent and anarchy in a democracy.We believe that the foundation of a vibrant democracy lies not merely in political equality, but also in economic and social justice. This principle underpins the decisions taken by our government.At the same time, for a stable and mature democracy it is important that dissent and concerns be expressed through legitimate and democratic channels, and resolved through dialogue and mutual understanding rather than by resorting to disorder.The need of the hour is to ensure that neither our democratic institutions nor India’s rise are held hostage to the frustration arising from political defeats. And, at no cost will the nation's progress be allowed to be undermined by those who would rather discredit the system than confront the reasons for their own setbacks.Rajnath Singh is the minister of defence, Government of India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Kenya reports 8th Ebola case as Congo outbreak expands across borders
articles.summary: Kenya confirmed its eighth Ebola case on Sunday after another person tested positive while in quarantine.
articles.body: Kenya confirmed its eighth Ebola case on Sunday after another person tested positive while in quarantine. Meanwhile, the outbreak in Congo spread to an eighth province, raising concerns over further cross-border transmission across the region.Kenya’s director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, said that a 49-year-old patient attendant had tested positive while in quarantine after being identified as a contact of the country’s first case."Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola," Amoth said in an interview with Kenya’s Citizen TV."He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain."According to Reuters, the man had attended to Kenya’s first Ebola patient, a 40-year-old Kenyan who travelled from DR Congo through Uganda and arrived in Kenya on October 3. The patient died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.Amoth said the latest patient had cleaned utensils and linens and was probably exposed to the first case. A health ministry source said he developed symptoms on Saturday and was isolated before testing positive on Sunday.Three close relatives of the first patient and three health workers have also tested positive. Authorities identified around 130 contacts following the initial death, with 128 remaining in quarantine. Six other patients were reported to be stable after receiving supportive treatment.Meanwhile, DR Congo’s health ministry confirmed two cases, including one death, in Nord-Ubangi province, which borders the Central African Republic. The development marks the outbreak’s spread to an eighth province, the Associated Press (AP) reported.Authorities have recorded at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history."We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out," World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told AP.Janabi identified reluctance among infected people to seek medical care as a major challenge, with some deaths occurring in communities outside health facilities."Ebola is a community disease. If the community does not cooperate, it will be very difficult," epidemiologist Serge Ngalebato said.Kenya has strengthened border screening, designated a gate at Nairobi’s main airport for flights from 10 high-risk countries and established an emergency hotline. Tanzania has also tightened screening and introduced 21-day monitoring for travellers from high-risk countries.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Villagers raised more than £311,000 to save a Cheshire pub shut for 12 years, combining community shares with £360,000 in government grants
articles.summary: For 12 years, the Golden Lion in Ashton Hayes, Cheshire, stood closed after the village pub shut in January 2013.
articles.body: For 12 years, the Golden Lion in Ashton Hayes, Cheshire, stood closed after the village pub shut in January 2013. Residents spent years campaigning to protect the historic building from redevelopment and return it to community use. Their efforts culminated in the purchase of the pub in June 2024 by Ashton Hayes Community Hub Ltd, a community benefit society. The project received £360,000 in government grants, while the society’s first annual general meeting report recorded £311,250 in community-share investment by early 2025. The building then underwent extensive restoration before reopening to customers on 7 August 2025. The campaign brought a long-closed village pub back into operation through a combination of public funding, local investment and sustained community organising.Golden Lion history: how Ashton Hayes campaigned to save its village pubThe Golden Lion closed in January 2013. Residents sought to protect the property from redevelopment and secure its future as a village pub. Its designation as an Asset of Community Value gave the community a route to pursue a purchase through the Right to Bid process. In 2016, residents formed the Golden Lion Working Group and began developing a plan to bring the property back into community ownership. They received guidance from the Plunkett Foundation, a charity that supports community-owned businesses. Ashton Hayes Community Hub Ltd was registered as a community benefit society in November 2017.An early attempt to buy the pub came in 2018. The society’s share prospectus records that an offer to the owner was supported by £196,100 in pledges from prospective investors. The offer was refused, and the pledged money was returned. The campaign continued for several years. After securing government funding and launching a new community-share offer, the society completed the purchase of the freehold on 14 June 2024 for £342,000, according to the society’s reports. The funding included a £250,000 capital grant and £92,000 from community-share funds.How community shares and £360,000 in grants funded the purchaseThe project combined government funding with investment from residents and other supporters. The government’s Community Ownership Fund awarded the society grants totalling £360,000. The funding table in the share prospectus breaks this down into a £250,000 capital grant, £60,000 for additional capital projects and a £50,000 revenue grant. The community-share offer launched at a public meeting on 2 May 2024. The society’s prospectus set an overall funding requirement of £625,000 to cover the purchase, refurbishment and initial operating costs. Its original minimum community-share target of £250,000 was subsequently reduced to £180,000 in an addendum, allowing the purchase to proceed while fundraising continued. The maximum subscription remained £420,000.The society’s website reported that the initial share offer had raised about £243,000 by August 2024, prompting an extension. Following that extension, the society’s first AGM report recorded a cumulative total of £311,250 by early 2025. The building’s condition created further challenges once restoration began. The society’s early-2025 report described structural problems and the need for additional funding. Work included stripping and re-slating the roof, addressing structural issues, adding insulation and replastering.The society’s chair’s report identified a funding shortfall of about £130,000 in early 2025 for the kitchen, cold storage and ventilation. The society’s website later reported that share funding had addressed the final funding gap needed to complete the kitchen, fire doors, lighting and furnishings. These costs added to the financial pressure as the society worked to bring the building back into use. The original prospectus also budgeted for replacement windows, electrical work, heating improvements and upgrades to the toilets and beer-pumping equipment. The early-2025 report does not confirm that all these budgeted items had been completed.The Golden Lion reopens after restorationThe pub reopened to customers on 7 August 2025, as reported by ITV News Granada and What’s Brewing. Its return followed more than a decade of closure and a restoration programme funded through the community purchase and subsequent fundraising. Lance Warburton became the tenant. The Chester Standard described him as having extensive experience managing pubs, restaurants and hotels across the country. The tenancy allows Ashton Hayes Community Hub Ltd to retain ownership of the building while a tenant manages its daily operation.The restoration also included improvements to the building’s access and infrastructure. In its early-2025 report, the society said a new pedestrian access path was in place and that the first-fix installation of the IT infrastructure had been completed. At that stage, a contract for the solar installation was about to be signed.Community investment and recognitionAshton Hayes Community Hub Ltd operates as a community benefit society. Interest is proposed by the Management Committee and put to a vote at the annual general meeting. Withdrawals, which can be requested after three years with three months’ notice, remain at the committee’s discretion. A tenant brief published by property agent Legat Owen reported that the society had more than 370 shareholders. Later coverage in 2026 described the number as having grown to more than 400.The project has received recognition beyond Ashton Hayes. CAMRA’s What’s Brewing covered the Golden Lion’s recognition as a runner-up in its Pub Saving Awards in January 2026. The awards coverage highlighted the community’s efforts to preserve the pub and restore it to use. The Golden Lion’s revival took years of campaigning, a government grant, community investment and extensive building work. Its reopening returned a historic pub to Ashton Hayes after 12 years of closure, with the building now owned by a community benefit society rather than dependent on a single private owner.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu will undertake a three-day state visit to Pakistan from Oct 20- 22, marking the first presidential visit from India’s
articles.body: Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu will undertake a three-day state visit to Pakistan from Oct 20- 22, marking the first presidential visit from India’s Indian Ocean neighbour to Islamabad in over a decade. The last president to visit Pakistan was the overly pro-China Abdulla Yameen. According to a press release issued by the president’s office in Male, Muizzu will hold talks with Pakistani PM Shehbaz Sharif and meet President Asif Ali Zardari.Reaffirming his foreign policy direction, the Maldives press release stressed Muizzu’s commitment to his “Maldives First” policy, prioritising strong regional partnerships to drive national development. The visit will be of concern to India, given its ongoing efforts to contribute to the Indian Ocean country’s financial stability. On the request of Maldives, India just carried out the first rollover of Rs 3000 crore currency swap, in line with an agreement signed in 2024. Muizzu’s call for revival of the Saarc summit process has also not gone unnoticed in India.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
