articles.title: Sex CDs, honeytraps and power: Why Karnataka politics keeps getting caught on camera
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A sleaze CD cost a minister his post in 2021. A trail of pen drives sent a former MP to prison for life in 2025.
articles.body: BENGALURU: A sleaze CD cost a minister his post in 2021. A trail of pen drives sent a former MP to prison for life in 2025. In between, legislators claimed in the House that dozens of their peers had been caught on camera. For nearly two decades now, Karnataka has seen a string of controversies involving alleged sexual misconduct, intimate recordings and blackmail, often making national headlines.One label has stuck, and the scandals have only grown in visibility and scale. Congress leader K N Rajanna, then cooperation minister, told the assembly in March 2025 that Karnataka was being called a factory of CDs and pen drives. He claimed 48 politicians had been honeytrapped, but named none.What the numbers sayThe latest allegations, involving political sting operations linked to former CM Siddaramaiah, have revived old questions. Why do such controversies keep surfacing here? Do they point to more sexual misconduct than in other states?Karnataka is often mistaken for the state with the most such cases. But a 2024 analysis of affidavits of 755 sitting MPs and 3,938 MLAs found that 151 had declared cases related to crimes against women, including rape.The analysis, by the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) and National Election Watch, shows West Bengal had 25 such legislators, Andhra 21 and Odisha 17. Karnataka was not in the top three.An earlier ADR analysis, on a different dataset, placed Karnataka seventh, with seven such legislators. West Bengal led with 26, followed by Maharashtra and Odisha with 14 each. The figures cover declared crimes against women, not necessarily sex scandals, leaked videos or proven misconduct. At the same time, it must be reiterated that a pending case is not proof of guilt.Timeline of Cases2024 | Prajwal Revanna’s pen-drive scandal- A major political storm broke out after sexually explicit videos allegedly involving former Hassan MP Prajwal Revanna surfaced in 2024. Several women filed complaints, leading to a special investigation team probe. In Aug 2025, a special court convicted Prajwal Revanna in one rape case and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The case remains one of Karnataka's most consequential sexual-abuse controversies.2021 | Ramesh Jarkiholi’s CD controversy- In March 2021, then water resources minister Ramesh Jarkiholi resigned after a video allegedly showing him with a woman surfaced. A complaint alleged that he had promised the woman a govt job in exchange for sexual favours. Jarkiholi denied wrongdoing and described the controversy as a conspiracy. The episode triggered political protests and demands for an investigation into the allegations.2019 | Arvind Limbavali’s video- In 2019, a purported video allegedly showing BJP MLA Arvind Limbavali in a compromising situation circulated and triggered a political controversy. Limbavali denied its authenticity and sought an investigation, claiming that he was being targeted. A forensic examination subsequently found the video to be fake.2016 | HY Meti’s resignation- In 2016, then excise minister HY Meti resigned after a purported video involving him and a woman triggered controversy. Allegations emerged that the woman had sought a favour relating to a job transfer. The woman subsequently withdrew her allegations, and the CID investigation ended without charges being established against Meti.2014 | SA Ramdas faces allegations- Former minister SA Ramdas faced allegations that he had sought sexual favours from a woman. Police registered a case following a complaint, and the controversy attracted significant attention. Ramdas denied wrongdoing. The Criminal Investigation Department subsequently cleared him of the allegations.2013 | Raghupathi Bhat’s video row- A purported video allegedly involving BJP MLA Raghupathi Bhat surfaced ahead of the Karnataka Assembly elections. The controversy drew attention because of its timing and the political implications for the legislator. Bhat subsequently withdrew from the electoral contest that year.2012 | Porn in the house- In 2012, Laxman Savadi, CC Patil and J Krishna Palemar, then ministers in the BJP govt, resigned after Savadi and Patil were caught watching explicit material on a mobile phone during assembly proceedings. A House committee recommended censure of Savadi but cleared the other two. A separate criminal complaint faced a procedural hurdle.2010 | Hartal Halappa’s rape case- In 2010, then Karnataka minister Hartal Halappa faced allegations that he had raped his friend's wife. He resigned later. The case attracted considerable attention because of his position in the BJP govt. Halappa denied the allegations and faced legal proceedings. A court acquitted him in 2017, citing insufficient evidence.2007 | Renukacharya’s controversy- BJP legislator Renukacharya faced allegations of sexual harassment from a nurse who claimed that he had pressured her to marry him. The controversy intensified after photographs of the two surfaced publicly. She later withdrew her case, bringing the legal controversy to a close.Why sex scandals repeatIt's arguable from the numbers that what sets Karnataka apart is visibility, not volume. The stakes are high, given the alleged involvement of prominent netas, ministerial exits, police probes, leaked recordings and how often the material becomes a political instrument.There are a few factors that make scandals a recurring theme in Karnataka politics.The first factor is the power imbalance. Legislators control a network of jobs, transfers and favours, potentially leaving those seeking favours vulnerable to exploitation.The Prajwal case, involving videos of women including domestic workers, party staff and govt personnel, highlighted how fear of political influence can delay complaints. The same access can also expose public figures to entrapment when encounters are recorded."When a minister's office controls postings, contracts and licences, consent is difficult to separate from the need to protect one's livelihood," says a retired IAS officer who has worked closely with senior politicians for over two decades.The second factor is rivalry. Compromising material becomes a weapon in struggles within parties, between factions, and between govt and opposition. Allegations involving recordings have repeatedly intersected with contests over ministerial berths, party leadership and electoral prospects.The latest episode has been linked by opposition leaders to a power struggle within the Congress, amid opposition efforts to exploit divisions in the governing party. Some allege the entrapment attempts were politically motivated; others say they were driven by financial blackmail. These remain allegations, not established findings."Their timing often coincides with cabinet expansions and leadership tussles," says political strategist MB Maramkal.The third is technology. A camera in every pocket turns a private act into a recording, and a recording into currency. The Prajwal case showed how explicit material could overshadow an election campaign, trigger police probes and prompt rival claims over who recorded and circulated the videos."Once a file is out, it cannot be recalled. Whoever holds a recording wields leverage even without publishing it. What a man records for control can be copied, leaked or sold by someone else, so the material that traps a victim can also trap the perpetrator," says Vishwanath Belliappa, a software professional.The flawed ‘honeytrap defence’Accused politicians often claim they were "honeytrapped", that is, deliberately lured into a compromising situation by rivals to be blackmailed or disgraced. This honeytrap defence has a corrosive side effect: genuine complaints get dismissed as conspiracy, and real victims become props in a factional fight.Both can be true: a trap can be political, and the conduct it exposes can still be criminal.The law asks what happened, not who gained from the exposure. "No single cause explains the recurrence. The decisive test is whether complaints are investigated impartially, digital evidence is forensically authenticated, victims and witnesses are protected, and allegations are settled through due process rather than political pressure," says Karnataka HC advocate Hidayathullah Kuvendu."Without that, such cases risk becoming political theatre instead of prosecutions, and without reliable comparative data, the state's notoriety may keep growing faster than the evidence to explain it. Karnataka's problem lies elsewhere: its politics treats scandals as ammunition first and crimes second."You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Bomb threat forces Tel Aviv to Vienna flight to land in Bulgaria
articles.summary: The Airbus jet landed safely in Bulgaria and all passengers and crew aboard were unharmed, officials said.
articles.body:
An Austrian Airlines flight from Israel to Austria has been forced to divert to Bulgaria after a reported bomb threat.

The Airbus A320 plane was travelling from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday night but made an emergency landing in Sofia, where passengers were evacuated, the Bulgarian transport ministry said in a statement.

The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner, the transport ministry said. No injuries have been reported and an investigation has begun.

It comes after a pilot attempted to hijack a Flydubai flight en route to Tel Aviv last month by attacking the captain, before the flight's crew and passengers overpowered him and landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

Bulgarian and Israeli media reported that a bomb threat had been made.

Austrian Airlines has confirmed a threat was made, without giving further details. A spokesperson told the AFP news agency there were 51 passengers and six crew members on board the jet.

Authorities conducted a security search of the plane after it landed in Sofia, about 30 minutes from when the alert was first raised. It was over Romania when it diverted to Sofia.

Flight tracking data showed Austrian Airlines 82 left Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv on Sunday evening before landing at Vasil Levski airport in Sofia three hours later.

Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.

The BBC has sought further comment from Lufthansa, the owner of Austrian Airlines.

articles.title: Meta’s ‘highest-paid employee’ Alexandr Wang on the WhatsApp message from Mark Zuckerberg that changed his career: Have time for a...
articles.summary: In April 2025, Alexandr Wang was sitting in a staff meeting at Scale AI, the data-labelling company he co-founded, when his phone pinged.
articles.body: In April 2025, Alexandr Wang was sitting in a staff meeting at Scale AI, the data-labelling company he co-founded, when his phone pinged. It was a WhatsApp message from Mark Zuckerberg: "Have time for a call?" Wang's first thought, as he tells it now, was simply, "huh, interesting."That call ran for 44 minutes. Within two months, Meta had put $14.3 billion into Scale AI for a 49% stake and brought Wang in to run its AI efforts. Wang and Zuckerberg retold the story together on Cheeky Pint, the podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison, in an episode recorded around the release of Meta's new Muse Wonder AI model.The timing of that message matters. Meta had released its Llama 4 models on April 4, 2025, to a lukewarm response. Around April 20, Zuckerberg said, he started calling people across the industry for advice on what to do next. Wang was one of them.Alexandr Wang's memo told Zuckerberg to hire fewer, better peopleTwo days after the call, Wang sent Zuckerberg a long memo. Zuckerberg described it on Cheeky Pint as Wang laying out what he would do "if I were in your position."The first point was about people, and how few of them Meta needed. "The very first thing is that you don't need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters," Zuckerberg recalled. That idea still shapes Meta Superintelligence Labs. Its core research team numbers under 200, "closer to 100," according to Wang, inside a company of roughly 75,000 employees.The hire raised eyebrows. Wang, now 29, is an MIT dropout who built Scale AI into a key data supplier for the big AI labs, but he had never trained a frontier model. Collison pointed this out on the show. Zuckerberg said he spoke to the heads of research at all the major labs before deciding, and came away sure: "Alex is the guy."What followed was a recruiting sprint Zuckerberg called "supernova." He cleared his calendar for a month or two just to meet researchers. "I don't think either of us slept that much for the first couple of months," he said.Wang also recalled one early meeting that left him uneasy. When he said Meta's first priority should be a strong reasoning model, one of the existing leads asked whether consumers needed one at all. Wang said he called Nat Friedman, now head of Meta's AI products, straight after.Meta's CFO warned Wang the AI bet had to workBy the end of 2025, the numbers had become enormous. Zuckerberg said Meta was preparing to "write this check for like, I don't know, like $100 billion, $200 billion" before anyone had seen the new models. "I'm like, Alex, are you sure this is going to work?"At an executive gathering in Hawaii, Wang said, CFO Susan Li pulled him aside several times to drive the point home. "If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad." Wang admitted that all he had to show at the time was a "vibe report" on research progress and a few plots.Muse and Muse Wonder have put Meta back in the AI raceThe bet produced Muse Spark in April 2026, followed by the Muse personal agent app on September 8. Muse climbed to the top of Apple's App Store within days. Wang's own Muse, which he named Oiler, buys increasingly obscure teas from farms in Taiwan and Japan every week. Zuckerberg uses his to critique his MMA technique in the one-minute breaks between rounds.On October 12, Meta released Muse Wonder, the first model it calls frontier-class. For now, it sits behind paid Muse subscriptions. Zuckerberg said the team was "very, very critical" of its own work along the way, and Wang describes the lab as a room full of "insecure overachievers."Asked what kind of boss Zuckerberg is, Wang called him "very Bayesian," someone who updates his beliefs and then moves the whole company to match. A five-word WhatsApp message, and the 44-minute call that followed, is about as clear an example of that as Meta has.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Psychology says children throw tantrums when parents are in a hurry, and it is not always stubbornness
articles.summary: The school bus is about to arrive, the tiffin is packed, and you are already running late for work.
articles.body: The school bus is about to arrive, the tiffin is packed, and you are already running late for work. But your toddler suddenly refuses to wear the shoes you have laid out, insists on a different water bottle or starts crying because you will not let them finish one more round of play. The more you hurry, the more they resist.For many Indian parents, this is a familiar morning struggle. Similar scenes unfold when it is time to leave a birthday party, switch off the television, get out of the park or hurry through a supermarket.It is easy to interpret these moments as stubbornness or deliberate defiance. But a young child's tantrum may have more to do with their still-developing ability to manage frustration than with an intention to make life difficult for a parent.Psychological research helps explain why transitions can be challenging for young children, how caregivers can support emotional regulation, and why a rushed situation may become harder when both parent and child are distressed.Importantly, research does not establish that parental hurry directly causes tantrums. Instead, it offers insights into the developmental and emotional factors that may make these moments difficult.Why a simple instruction can trigger a big reactionFor an adult, leaving the playground means stopping one activity and moving on to the next. For a child, it could mean giving up a favourite game, leaving friends behind or accepting that something enjoyable has ended before they were ready.Young children are also developing executive function: the mental skills involved in controlling impulses, shifting attention, planning and adapting to change.Harvard University's Center on the Developing Child explains how executive function develops. These skills do not emerge fully formed in early childhood. Children gradually learn to manage competing demands, change focus and control their immediate reactions. Imagine asking a three-year-old to stop building a tower, put away the blocks and get ready for school. The child must disengage from an absorbing activity, accept the interruption and cooperate with a new routine. When the child is already tired or frustrated, managing all these demands can become harder.A 2023 study published in Infant Behavior and Development, involving 197 families, found that executive function at 14 months predicted aspects of emotional regulation during mother-child play at 24 months. The association was not found in observations involving fathers, highlighting the relationship-specific nature of the findings.The study, Developmental Links Between Executive Function and Emotion Regulation in Early Toddlerhood, does not examine rushed mornings, but it illustrates how children's developing cognitive skills are connected with their ability to manage emotions.A tantrum, therefore, may reflect difficulty coping with a frustrating situation rather than a calculated attempt to challenge parental authority.When the parent's urgency adds to the tensionConsider a typical morning in an Indian household. A parent has an important work meeting, the school bus is expected shortly, and the child refuses to put on their uniform. The parent repeats the instruction, the child begins crying, and the parent responds more sharply. Soon, a disagreement over getting dressed becomes a full-blown meltdown.The parent is anxious about being late; the child is upset about the immediate demand. Neither may have the emotional space to respond calmly.This is where the concept of co-regulation becomes useful. It refers to the support caregivers provide as children learn to manage their emotions and behaviour.Research published in 2023 on executive function and emotional regulation supports the importance of considering the caregiver-child relationship when understanding how these skills develop. Parents cannot regulate every emotion for their children, but they can help them navigate distress through predictable routines, supportive responses and clear boundaries.A parent who says, “I know you want to keep playing. It is difficult to stop, but we have to leave now,” communicates both understanding and a limit. Repeatedly shouting “Hurry up!” may communicate urgency without helping the child manage the disappointment.This does not mean parents must remain perfectly calm or that a child will stop crying if spoken to gently. It means that increasing the pressure is not necessarily the same as helping the child cooperate.What research says about tantrumsTantrums are common in early childhood, but their frequency, duration and intensity can vary.A 2022 longitudinal study published in the Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics examined parent reports of tantrums among 861 children aged one to five years. A smaller group was followed up approximately a year later.Researchers found that tantrum frequency generally declined with age, while duration increased across the age range studied. More frequent tantrums predicted more externalising problems, while longer tantrums predicted internalising problems in the follow-up analyses.These findings should not be used to label an occasional meltdown as a warning sign. They show why it is important to consider the overall pattern of behaviour rather than judge a child by one difficult morning.Another study, published in 2023 in Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology, followed 94 toddlers over a year and examined parenting approaches alongside observed tantrum severity. The researchers found that greater use of power assertion and less consistency predicted increases in tantrum severity over time.The study, Parental Discipline Techniques and Changes in Observed Temper Tantrum Severity in Toddlers, suggests that the way adults respond to challenging behaviour may matter. However, its relatively small sample means the findings should be interpreted cautiously.Taken together, this research supports a balanced approach: acknowledge children's distress, maintain appropriate boundaries and avoid assuming that every tantrum is deliberate misbehaviour.How parents can handle tantrums when they are running late1. Acknowledge the feeling without changing the boundaryInstead of saying, “Stop crying, we are already late,” try: “You wanted to play longer. I know you are upset. Now we have to go.”This recognises the child's disappointment without suggesting that crying will cancel the departure.2. Give a small choice“Do you want to wear the blue shoes or the red ones?” gives the child some control while keeping the decision manageable.This can be more helpful than turning the moment into a long negotiation. Offer choices only when both options are acceptable.3. Give advance warningsAt the park, tell your child, “Five more minutes, then we are going home,” and give another reminder when the time is nearly up.A warning cannot guarantee a tantrum-free departure, but it gives the child an opportunity to prepare for the transition rather than experience it as an abrupt interruption.4. Use fewer words during the tantrumWhen a child is highly distressed, a lengthy explanation about punctuality or responsibility is unlikely to be useful in that moment. Keep your words simple: “You are upset. I am here. We need to get ready.”Prioritise safety and help the child settle before discussing what happened.5. Make the routine less rushed where possiblePack school bags, prepare clothes and organise essentials the previous evening. Build a little extra time into departures when feasible.These changes will not eliminate tantrums, but they may reduce the number of last-minute demands placed on both parent and child.What if the tantrum happens in public?A child screaming at a supermarket checkout or refusing to leave a birthday party can make a parent feel judged by everyone around them. That pressure may create an additional urge to stop the behaviour immediately.Try to separate the child's distress from the reactions of bystanders. If possible, move to a quieter, safer place and speak calmly. If it is time to leave, maintain the boundary while offering comfort.There is no need to turn the episode into a public lecture about obedience. Once the child is calmer, you can talk about what happened and practise a more manageable way to handle the transition next time.When should parents seek help?Parents should consider consulting a paediatrician or child mental health professional if tantrums are persistently intense, unusually prolonged, involve repeated injury to the child or others, significantly disrupt everyday life, or occur alongside other developmental concerns.The important consideration is the pattern, not one isolated episode.The takeawayWhen a child throws a tantrum just as the family is running late, it can feel as though they have chosen the worst possible moment to resist. But understanding the demands of emotional regulation can help parents see the situation differently.The school bus may not wait, the family may have to leave the park, and the television still needs to be switched off. Boundaries remain important.The aim is not to prevent every tantrum or give in to every demand. It is to help children gradually learn to handle disappointment and transitions without turning every difficult feeling into a battle.Sometimes, the most useful response is to hold the boundary firmly while remembering that a child who is struggling to cope is not necessarily trying to make things harder.You use AI every day. articles.title: Can technology prevent the next stampede? Inside the crowd-monitoring tools India needs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nineteen people were killed and 25 injured in the stampede at Kolkata’s Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on Saturday, bringing crowd management back
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nineteen people were killed and 25 injured in the stampede at Kolkata’s Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on Saturday, bringing crowd management back into focus.Heavy rain was said to have driven visitors toward the entrance, causing a stampede in which people fell over each other. The tragedy raises an important question: can technology identify the warning signs before a crowd turns dangerous?Predicting disaster to documentingIndia has invested heavily in CCTV cameras in public places, transport hubs and mass gatherings. But cameras that just record events are of little use in preventing a stampede. Artificial intelligence (AI) can analyze live video feeds, estimate crowd density, track movement and flag sudden surges, so control rooms can identify trouble spots before conditions become critical. The challenge is to turn surveillance into an early warning system that leads to action.AI cameras can detect crowd build-upSuch systems can count people entering and exiting a venue, map congestion at individual gates and identify areas where flow has slowed or reversed.Algorithms can also spot unusual clustering, sudden changes in the direction of crowds and people falling. During the 2025 Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj, an integrated command and control center was deployed to monitor crowd density and movement utilizing inputs from 500 AI-enabled cameras and drones.How alerts are only usefulA monitoring system has to be more than just flashing a warning on a screen. Alerts should be sent to police officers, event organizers and teams managing entry and exit points when density exceeds a pre-set safety threshold. Officials may be able to temporarily stop incoming visitors, create designated dispersal routes, redirect people from choke points or place personnel to relieve pressure. Importantly, thresholds should be based on the layout of the venue and the patterns of movement, not on a single crowd-count figure.Access clear announcementsDigital ticketing, people counters and entry gates fed with live occupancy data can help organizers prevent a venue from exceeding its safe capacity. Connect public address systems to crowd-control teams so instructions are consistent as conditions change. Heavy rain is said to have contributed to the rush. It could also lead to weather alerts and precautionary measures at Kolkata. These may include temporary entry restrictions, additional personnel deployment, and clear directions for visitors.Tech can't replace ground level planningEven the most sophisticated artificial intelligence can't make up for narrow exits, badly placed barricades or insufficient evacuation plans. Cameras can also fail to capture activity in blind spots and can be affected by rain, poor lighting or dense crowds, which can affect the quality of readings. So every major event needs a physical safety audit, clearly marked emergency routes, trained personnel and medical teams and regular evacuation drills. Technology should reinforce these arrangements, not give a false sense of security.Next step: real-time crowd safety networkIndia needs a common operating framework for high-footfall religious gatherings, festivals, railroad stations and public events connecting CCTV analytics, entry counts, weather alerts and emergency response teams.Authorities should also carry out post-event audits to determine if alerts were issued and acted on in a timely manner. As adoption grows, privacy protections and independent verification of automated systems will be critical.
